Skyline Travel Log — Privacy Policy

Last updated: 5 September 2026

Skyline Travel Log (“SkyLine” on your Home screen) logs the flights you have taken and draws them on a globe. This policy describes exactly what the app does with your information. It is written against the app’s actual behaviour, not a template.

The short version

  • Your flights are stored in your own iCloud account, not on our servers. We cannot read them.
  • When you scan a boarding pass, the app first tries to read the barcode on your device. Nothing leaves your phone when that works.
  • If there is no readable barcode, the image is sent to an AI service to be read. A boarding pass image can contain your name and booking reference.
  • Deleting your account removes your data and revokes Sign in with Apple, so SkyLine stops appearing under your Apple Account. See below.
  • We do not use analytics, advertising, or tracking of any kind.

What we collect, and where it goes

Your flights

Flights you add — by scanning or by typing them in — are written to the private database of your own iCloud account (CloudKit container iCloud.com.skyline.flighttracker). This is storage that belongs to you. The developer has no access to it, and it is covered by Apple’s iCloud privacy terms.

Deleting the app does not delete this data. To remove it, use Settings → Delete Account inside SkyLine.

Boarding pass and confirmation images

When you scan a pass, SkyLine tries three things in order:

  1. Barcode, on your device. Most printed boarding passes carry a PDF417 barcode holding the flight details in a standard format. This is decoded entirely on your phone. Nothing is transmitted.
  2. If no barcode can be read, the image is uploaded. This happens with booking confirmations, emailed itineraries, screenshots that crop the barcode out, and passes issued before check-in. The image travels to a Cloudflare Worker operated by the developer, and from there to OpenRouter, which passes it to OpenAI’s GPT-4o to be read. Alongside the image we send the identifier Apple gives the app for your account, used only to rate-limit abuse of that endpoint. The Worker keeps that identifier as a daily request count for 24 hours and then it expires. Nothing else about you is stored there, and the image itself is not.
  3. On-device text recognition, as a last resort — Apple’s Vision framework reads the text off the image and Apple Intelligence’s on-device model turns it into flight fields. Nothing is transmitted.

One other request leaves the app, and only when you ask for it: deleting your account sends a single-use Apple authorization code to that same Worker, so your Sign in with Apple credential can be revoked. See Deleting your account below.

What that image can contain. A boarding pass typically shows your name, the booking reference (PNR), flight number, route, date, seat, and sometimes a frequent-flyer number. If you would rather none of that leave your device, do not scan documents without a barcode — use Enter manually instead, which transmits nothing.

Images are sent for the sole purpose of reading the flight out of them. They are not stored by us after the response is returned. We do not control OpenRouter’s or OpenAI’s retention; see their policies, linked above.

Airport and airline lookups

To draw a route we need coordinates for an airport code, and a name for an airline code. The two work differently, so they are described separately.

Airports. Coordinates come from a table of just over nine thousand airports shipped inside the app. Looking one up sends nothing anywhere: it reads a file already on your phone, and it works with no network at all.

Airlines. Airline names come from a short list built into the app, covering the carriers SkyLine was built and tested against. A code that is not on that list is looked up in the private database of your own iCloud account — the same storage your flights live in, described above — and once resolved it is written back there and cached on your device, so the lookup does not repeat. The app also writes a handful of well-known airline records into that private database the first time you sign in. Those requests go to Apple’s iCloud on your behalf, not to us.

No third-party service is contacted to identify an airport or an airline, and nothing about your flights is sent to one.

Sign in with Apple

SkyLine requires an account. Apple gives the app a stable identifier for you, and your name and email if you choose to share them. These are held on your device and in your own iCloud record. The identifier is also sent with image scans, as described above, for rate limiting.

You can delete your account at any time from Settings → Delete Account. This removes your flights from iCloud and clears the app’s local data.

It also revokes your Sign in with Apple credential, so SkyLine stops being listed under your Apple Account. Apple requires this, and it is not something an app can do by itself: revoking a credential has to be signed with a key that belongs to the developer account, and a key like that cannot safely live inside an app. So at the moment you confirm deletion, SkyLine asks Apple for a fresh, single-use authorization code and sends only that code to the same Cloudflare Worker described above, which holds the signing key and asks Apple to revoke. The code is used once and is not stored, by the Worker or by us. Nothing about your flights is involved.

If that request fails — no network, say — the deletion still goes ahead and your data is still removed. The app tells you so, and you can finish the job yourself in the iOS Settings app → your name → Sign in with Apple → SkyLine → Stop using Apple ID.

Photos

SkyLine uses the system photo picker. It receives only the single image you choose. The app has no access to the rest of your photo library and never requests it.

What we do not do

  • No analytics or crash-reporting SDKs. There are none in the app.
  • No advertising, and no advertising identifiers.
  • No tracking across apps or websites. Nothing is shared with data brokers.
  • No selling of data. The only thing held on the developer’s own infrastructure is the 24-hour request counter described above; your flights are never on it, and there is nothing there to sell.

Children

SkyLine is not directed at children under 13 and does not knowingly collect their information.

Changes

If this policy changes, the date at the top changes with it, and the updated version will be published at this address.
